flags.description: Exports to China rose from 12% to 32% of manganese exports between 2007 and 2008 (reported by BRA to UN Comtrade).
Exports to China rose from 25% to 50% of the country's mineral exports between 2008 and 2009 (reported by BRA to UN Comtrade).
Exports to China fell from 23% to under 0.1% of nickel exports between 2009 and 2010 (reported by BRA to UN Comtrade).
Exports to the United States rose from 18% to 44% of tin exports between 2011 and 2012 (reported by BRA to UN Comtrade).
Exports to China fell from 79% to 46% of manganese exports between 2020 and 2021 (reported by BRA to UN Comtrade).

Legislative stance toward China in 2025 (22 scored records) was cooler than the movement of economic ties would suggest (gap -2.2 standard deviations); the stance values come from the text model (zero-shot baseline, not yet validated).

sentences.text: In 2024, the influence index stands at 34.9 for China (band 28.8–50.8, from 5 of six components) and 7.0 for the United States (band 4.8–43.5, from 4 of six components). The net lean is +27.9 points toward China.
Over the five years to 2024, the index for China rose by 8.5 points and the index for the United States fell by 7.9 points.

The value for China rests on trade export share, trade import share, debt stock, diplomatic alignment and legislative stance; every component is a recorded tie (trade shares, finance, debt, UN votes, legislative stance), not a judgement.

The value for the United States rests on trade export share, trade import share, finance flow and diplomatic alignment; every component is a recorded tie (trade shares, finance, debt, UN votes, legislative stance), not a judgement.
In 2025, 48% of Brazil's mineral exports (UN Comtrade value US$47.2 bn) went to China and 2.6% to the United States; together 50%, the rest to other destinations.
Since 2020 the share going to China fell by 8.1 points and the share going to the United States was broadly flat.
Relative to the 20-country export basket, its exports are specialised in niobium (RCA 3.2), titanium (RCA 3.1) and bauxite aluminum (RCA 3.0).

5 sudden shifts in export shares are flagged from the customs data, the latest in 2021: Exports to China fell from 79% to 46% of manganese exports between 2020 and 2021 (reported by BRA to UN Comtrade).

human.title: Brazil: iron ore sets the dependence, rare earths set the conversation
human.author: AI-drafted from the site's indicators; not yet reviewed by the project owner
human.text_md:
## Alignment

Brazil's index leans toward China, 27.0 against 12.7 in 2025, on three and four components (36.3 against 6.9 in 2024, when UN voting and debt were still in the Chinese value) [index_value:influence:CN:2025] [index_value:influence:US:2025] [index_value:influence:CN:2024]. The lean is made of iron ore: of US$47.2 bn of mineral exports in 2025, 48% went to China and 2.6% to the United States, and China took US$19.5 bn of the US$29.0 bn of iron ore [concentration:share_cn_x:2025] [flow_trade:BRA:iron_ore:2025]. The executives' coded statements are the coolest toward both powers among the larger countries, +0.08 toward the United States over thirteen statements and 0.00 toward China over four, with four coded negatives toward the United States and one toward China [statement:stance_us:BRA:2024-2026] [statement:stance_cn:BRA:2024-2026]. Rare earths take 57% of the mineral mentions in Brazilian statements and 0.0% of the export value; iron ore is 61% of the value and a tenth of the mentions, one of the largest mismatches in the region at 0.80 [insights:talk_vs_trade_minerals:BRA]. My reading: Brazil talks about the minerals of the next decade in the language of sovereignty, and sells the minerals of this one to China.

## Trajectory

The Chinese share of exports rose from 25% in 2008 to 41% in 2012 and 56% in 2020, then fell back to 48% in 2025 [concentration:share_cn_x:2020] [concentration:share_cn_x:2025]. Chinese commitments were the largest among the trading countries, US$28.8 bn over 2015–2021 with US$8.2 bn in each of 2015 and 2016, most of it outside mining [flow_finance:CN:BRA:2015-2021]; US DFC and EXIM commitments were US$1.3 bn in the same years and US$0.9 bn in 2022–2024 [flow_finance:US:BRA:2015-2021] [flow_finance:US:BRA:2022-2024]. The say–do series is one of only two in the region: in 2025 the legislature's rhetoric toward the United States ran slightly cooler than the recorded ties (gap −0.2 standard deviations over 15 records) [say_do_gap:US:BRA:2025]. Against the countries outside its scope, the Chancay port opening of November 2024 is followed by a 10.2-point fall in the share to China, the opposite of what a Pacific gateway would suggest, with a permutation p of 0.25 [event_effect:per_chancay_port_opening:CN:did:BRA]. The legislature's coded records lean positive toward both powers (2025: +0.18 toward China and +0.60 toward the United States; 2026: +0.40 over 23 records and +0.27) [document:stance_cn:BRA:2025] [document:stance_us:BRA:2026].

## Risks and likely next moves

The models put China's share at 55% in 2030 at baseline, 65% under the China pull and 45% under US reshoring; the US share reaches 13% only under reshoring [forecast:export_share:CN:us_reshoring:2030:BRA] [forecast:export_share:US:us_reshoring:2030:BRA]. Parity would take US$10.7 bn of yearly exports switching, 8.8 times what the United States bought in 2025; iron ore alone could cover it, nothing else could [insights:parity_gap:BRA]. The law of 16 September 2026 creating the national critical-minerals policy and its council is the next move already made [event:bra_lei_15506_critical_minerals]; in my reading it will shape where rare earths, niobium and graphite go in the 2030s, not where iron ore goes in the 2020s. The risk for the reading is a steel-demand shift in China that moves the iron-ore share for reasons that have nothing to do with policy.

## What would change this reading

A 2026 trade year in which iron ore to China fell below 60% of the mineral; DFC or EXIM commitments to Brazilian rare-earth or niobium projects; a reviewed event list that confirmed or dropped the Chancay window; or a second coder who read Lula's statements on the United States as something other than negative.
